evidence.claim: The present M-15 designation began after 1926 on a highway from Clarkston to Vassar.
evidence.quote: The current routing of M-15 was designated after 1926. The southern end was located at US 10 in Clarkston running north to M-38 and M-24 in Vassar.

evidence.claim: By the end of 1936 it extended into Bay City, sharing M-24’s route.
evidence.quote: By the end of 1936, M-15 was extended concurrently along M-24 from Vassar into Bay City.

evidence.claim: Further extensions carried the number across Bay City to the freeway, but those were reversed in 1970.
evidence.quote: This M-15/M-25 routing was extended again in the next year to end at the new I-75/US 10/US 23 freeway. These two northerly extensions were both reversed and scaled back in 1970.

evidence.claim: The northern end returned to Center Avenue, where it remains.
evidence.quote: M-15's northern end is moved back to M-25/Center Avenue in Bay City, its current location.

evidence.claim: A dam was part of the founders’ plan: James M. Edmunds and Townsend North led four men seeking a place to build one and establish a city.
evidence.quote: Vassar was founded by four men who were led by James M. Edmunds and Townsend North in search of an area to build a dam and start a city.

evidence.claim: They named Vassar for Edmunds’ uncle Matthew, later the founder of Vassar College.
evidence.quote: The city was named after Edmunds' uncle, Matthew Vassar, who later founded Vassar College.

evidence.claim: The county seat moved to Caro in 1860, while lumbering and related industries drove Vassar’s growth for the next thirty years.
evidence.quote: In 1860, the seat was moved to Caro. Vassar's growth for the next thirty years was based mainly on its lumbering and a handful of related industries.

evidence.claim: North’s ventures included a sawmill in 1849 and a woolen mill in 1867.
evidence.quote: He established the first sawmill in 1849, selling it in 1865. He founded a woolen mill in 1867

evidence.claim: After timber depletion and the 1881 Thumb Fire, the area shifted toward agriculture, with sugar beets important to its economy by 1900.
evidence.quote: the depletion of the timberlands in the area and the 1881 Thumb Fire signalled the end of lumbering in Vassar. The area shifted to agricultural production, particularly of sugar beets. By 1900, sugar beet production was an important component of the local economy.

evidence.claim: Ortonville grew at a milling center established by Amos Orton.
evidence.quote: The small community of Ortonville grew up around the milling center

evidence.claim: He built a gristmill in 1852 and replaced it in 1856 with the structure at 366 Mill Street.
evidence.quote: In 1852, he constructed a gristmill nearby to make the location more attractive to potential settlers. In 1856, he replaced the gristmill with the current structure.

evidence.claim: He built a gristmill in 1852 and replaced it in 1856 with the structure at 366 Mill Street.
evidence.quote: The  Ortonville Mill  is a former gristmill located at 366 Mill Street in Ortonville, Michigan.

evidence.claim: Orton combined milling with work as a blacksmith and storekeeper, making the mill site a center for several of the settlement’s trades.
evidence.quote: The small community of Ortonville grew up around the milling center, with Amos Orton working as the miller, blacksmith, and keeping a general store.

evidence.claim: The mill adopted roller processing in 1889 and generated electricity for the community during part of the 1920s.
evidence.quote: In 1889, the mill was converted to the roller process, and for a time during the 1920s also generated electric power for the community.

evidence.claim: Milling continued until 1960.
evidence.quote: The mill continued in use until 1960

evidence.claim: Emiline and Jack Hamilton donated the building to the Ortonville Community Historical Society in 1968.
evidence.quote: In 1968, Emiline and Jack Hamilton donated the Mill to the Ortonville Community Historical Society for use as a museum of local history.

evidence.claim: The hand-hewn timber-frame mill now serves as a local-history museum.
evidence.quote: The Ortonville Community Historical Society now operates the mill as a museum of local history.

evidence.claim: The mill is a timber-frame, two-and-a-half-story Greek Revival building.
evidence.quote: The Ortonville Mill is a 2-1/2 story Greek Revival structure, made with a hand-hewn timber frame
